subject: science
title: KS3 Science Reading — Biology: Variation and Inheritance
subtitle: Reading passages and comprehension questions for KS3 Biology variation and inheritance.
description: Five short KS3 reading passages on variation, inheritance, adaptation, selective breeding, extinction and scientific data. Questions test retrieval, inference, explanation and use of evidence from values.

data.sourcePassage: Variation means the differences between individuals of the same species. In one class, students may differ in height, hand span, natural hair colour, eye colour, reaction time and learned skills. In a garden, plants of the same species may vary in height, leaf length, flower colour and growth rate. Some variation is inherited from genetic information passed from parents to offspring. Some variation is environmental, caused by surroundings or experiences such as light, water, diet, injury or learning. Many characteristics, such as height and body mass, are affected by both inherited and environmental factors.

questions.question: What does variation mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Variation means differences between individuals of the same species.

questions.question: Which example is mostly environmental variation?
questions.modelAnswer: A scar from an accident.

questions.question: Why is height often described as affected by both inherited and environmental factors?
questions.modelAnswer: Genetic information can affect potential height, while diet, health and other conditions during growth can affect the final height reached.

questions.question: Why should students avoid judging a person from inherited characteristics?
questions.modelAnswer: Inherited characteristics do not show a person's worth, ability, identity or future, and respectful data handling is important.

questions.question: Which pair best contrasts inherited and environmental variation?
questions.modelAnswer: Inherited variation comes from DNA from parents, while environmental variation comes from conditions during life.
options: DNA from parents versus conditions during life

data.sourcePassage: Continuous variation has values across a range and is usually measured using numbers and units. Height, body mass, hand span, leaf length, reaction time and running speed are examples. Discontinuous variation falls into separate categories or groups and is usually counted. Blood group, eye colour categories, attached or detached earlobes and some flower colour categories are examples. A common mistake is to treat measurements as fixed groups only, or to join category bars with a line as if there are values between categories.

questions.question: Give one example of continuous variation from the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include height, body mass, hand span, leaf length, reaction time or running speed.

questions.question: Give one example of discontinuous variation from the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include blood group, eye colour category, attached or detached earlobes, or flower colour category.

questions.question: Why is a bar chart suitable for eye colour categories?
questions.modelAnswer: A bar chart is suitable because eye colour categories are separate groups.
options: Eye colour is measured in centimetres
A line must join all bars

questions.question: Explain why joining category bars with a line can be misleading.
questions.modelAnswer: It suggests there are continuous values between the categories, but categories such as blue and brown eye colour are separate groups.

questions.question: A class groups hand span measurements into intervals. Why can this still be continuous variation?
questions.modelAnswer: The original hand span values are measured across a range in centimetres; grouping them into intervals is only a way to display the measured data.

data.sourcePassage: Most body cells contain a nucleus. The nucleus contains chromosomes, which are long structures made of DNA. DNA is a chemical that carries genetic information. A gene is a short section of DNA with instructions for a particular inherited characteristic. During reproduction, genetic information is passed from parents to offspring. Offspring often resemble their parents because they receive genetic information from them, but they are not usually identical because they receive a mixture of information and their environment can also affect how some characteristics develop.

questions.question: Where are chromosomes found in most body cells?
questions.modelAnswer: Chromosomes are found in the nucleus of most body cells.

questions.question: What are chromosomes made from?
questions.modelAnswer: Chromosomes are made from DNA.

questions.question: What is a gene?
questions.modelAnswer: A gene is a short section of DNA with instructions for a particular inherited characteristic.

questions.question: Why do offspring often resemble their parents?
questions.modelAnswer: They inherit genetic information from their parents during reproduction.

questions.question: Why are offspring not usually identical to either parent?
questions.modelAnswer: They receive a mixture of genetic information and some characteristics are also affected by environmental factors.

data.sourcePassage: An adaptation is a feature or behaviour that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment. Adaptations may be structural, such as thick fur or cactus spines; behavioural, such as migration or hibernation; or physiological, such as conserving water. Adaptations do not appear instantly because an organism needs them. Helpful inherited features can become more common over many generations if individuals with those features survive and reproduce. Selective breeding is different: humans choose parents with useful inherited characteristics and breed them, then select the best offspring and repeat the process over generations.

questions.question: What is an adaptation?
questions.modelAnswer: An adaptation is a feature or behaviour that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment.

questions.question: Which is a behavioural adaptation?
questions.modelAnswer: Migration is a behavioural adaptation because it is an action.

questions.question: Why do adaptations usually become common over many generations rather than appearing instantly?
questions.modelAnswer: Individuals with helpful inherited features are more likely to survive and reproduce, so those features can become more common in the population over generations.

questions.question: What do humans choose in selective breeding?
questions.modelAnswer: Humans choose parents with useful inherited characteristics.

questions.question: Give one benefit and one risk of selective breeding.
questions.modelAnswer: A benefit is improved food production or disease resistance. A risk is reduced genetic variation or inherited health problems.

data.sourcePassage: Extinction is the permanent disappearance of a species when no living members remain anywhere on Earth. Extinction risk can increase because of rapid environmental change, habitat loss, climate change, pollution, overhunting, disease, competition, lack of food and failure to reproduce successfully. In one wetland bird data set, wetland habitat area fell from 120 hectares in 2022 to 52 hectares in 2025. Breeding pairs fell from 80 to 31, and chicks surviving to autumn fell from 96 to 21. This suggests increasing extinction risk because fewer adults are breeding and fewer young birds are surviving to replace adults that die.

questions.question: By how much did wetland habitat area fall between 2022 and 2025?
questions.modelAnswer: It fell by 68 hectares, from 120 hectares to 52 hectares.

questions.question: Which trend was shown by breeding pairs?
questions.modelAnswer: Breeding pairs fell from 80 to 31.

questions.question: Use the chick survival values to explain why extinction risk may be increasing.
questions.modelAnswer: Chicks surviving to autumn fell from 96 to 21, so fewer young birds are replacing adults that die.

questions.question: Give one conservation action and one limitation of the wetland bird data.
questions.modelAnswer: A conservation action could be protecting and restoring wetland habitat. A limitation is that the data does not show disease, predators, food supply, weather or pollution.
